The basic sequence is to put the fingers on the touch-sensitive neoprene playing surface, move along its length for continuous pitch, move across its width to change timbre, press perpendicularly to change volume, and send the pressure values to a digital music interface. A beginner should first practise glissando, vibrato and pitch bending with one finger, then use the software's rounding to align the pitch with twelve-tone equal temperament, just intonation or another scale, and finally practise several voices by touching the surface with several fingers at once.

The surface senses finger position and pressure; along the length the pitch changes continuously, which allows glissando, vibrato, pitch bending and non-chromatic pitches; the full-size instrument spans about 7.79 octaves and the half-size about 3.84. Position across the width can change the timbre, and perpendicular pressure corresponds to changes in volume or amplitude, with up to sixteen voices sounding at once. Compared with a traditional keyboard of fixed pitches, it does not switch pitch by key but affects the synthesis parameters directly through continuous touch.

The Continuum Fingerboard is an electrophone, and also a musical performance controller and synthesiser, developed by Lippold Haken and sold by Haken Audio. Its playing surface is a touch-sensitive neoprene slab; sensors detect finger position and pressure, so that pitch, timbre and volume can change continuously, and it controls a synthesiser through a digital music interface or an audio output. The player slides and presses fingers on the surface, unlike a piano keyboard. It is used in modern music, film and game scores and live performance, for example by Jordan Rudess, A. R. Rahman and Hans Zimmer.
